To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a computer vision system can learn to classify leaves into botanical families and orders using a database of 2,001 leaf images from 7,597 specimens, and that the resulting system can classify novel leaf images into families and/or orders with an accuracy that is many times greater than that of chance.

we have demonstrated that a computer vision algorithm can learn features of botanical orders and families from a database of cleared and stained leaf specimens and then classify novel images of cleared leaves into families and orders.
machine learning can be used to learn a set of features from a large number of images of cleared leaves, and to classify novel images into botanical families and orders.

this is the first demonstration of computer vision learning features of botanical families or orders, and that the results have direct relevance to systematic studies.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we developed a computer vision algorithm that can learn to recognize and classify leaves from major evolutionary groups.
the leaf images are not just pictures, but a new source of information that can be used in phylogeny reconstruction and other systematic studies.

the machine learning algorithm learned to identify the major families and orders of angiosperms from their leaves with a success rate of 75% and 60% respectively, and that the algorithm can identify the major families of angiosperms with a success rate greater than 80% from a single leaf image.
The main takeaway from our work is that
computer vision is a powerful tool that is ready to be applied to a broad range of problems in botany.
the visual features of leaves, even at the level of families and orders, are highly predictable.
